title: Aesthetics and psychobiology
authority: Berlyne founded the modern experimental psychology of aesthetics; this book is its canonical statement of arousal-potential theory.
caveats: The inverted-U between complexity and liking is supported in many studies but not universal; effects depend on stimulus class, expertise and context. Meta-analyses find modest, variable support.

title: Attitudinal effects of mere exposure
container: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology Monograph Supplement
authority: Zajonc was a leading social psychologist; this monograph is the founding paper of the mere exposure effect.
caveats: A large meta-analysis (Bornstein 1989) supports a small to moderate effect, but it weakens or reverses with excessive repetition, complex stimuli and strong prior attitudes. Bibliographic details confirmed by search; DOI removed as not confirmed.

title: Processing fluency and aesthetic pleasure: Is beauty in the perceiver's processing experience?
authority: Leading social-cognition researchers; the standard review linking fluency to beauty.
caveats: Fluency effects are real but modest; novelty and disfluency can also raise interest. Some predictions (e.g. prototypicality always preferred) are contested. DOI removed as not confirmed.

title: 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design
authority: Delft and Amsterdam design psychologists; empirical test of Raymond Loewy's MAYA principle.
caveats: Stimuli were consumer product categories with limited item sets; novelty and typicality were strongly negatively correlated, so separating them is hard. DOI removed as not confirmed.

title: A model of aesthetic appreciation and aesthetic judgments
authority: Vienna empirical aesthetics group; the most cited information-processing model of aesthetic experience.
caveats: Developed for art; applied to websites by extension. Leder and Nadal (2014) revised it, and Leder (2013) argued it underplays emotion.

title: What is beautiful is usable
authority: Origin of the aesthetic-usability effect in HCI, building on Kurosu and Kashimura (1995).
caveats: Simulated ATM layouts, student sample; Tuch et al. (2012) found the reverse under some conditions. Treat as perception, not performance.

title: Is beautiful really usable? Toward understanding the relation between usability, aesthetics, and affect in HCI
authority: Basel HCI group, peer-reviewed controlled experiment that qualifies the aesthetic-usability effect.
caveats: One online shop, 80 participants. Author list varies across indexes (some omit Bargas-Avila). DOI removed as not confirmed.

title: Assessing dimensions of perceived visual aesthetics of web sites
authority: Foundational scale development paper for perceived web aesthetics.
caveats: Moshagen and Thielsch (2010) criticised some items (e.g. symmetrical, special effects) as not aesthetic judgments.

title: Facets of visual aesthetics
authority: Psychometric development of VisAWI across seven studies; widely used instrument.
caveats: Perception instrument, not behavior. The four facet names (simplicity, diversity, colorfulness, craftsmanship) are from the VisAWI literature; only craftsmanship was quoted in this session's search results.

title: The interplay of beauty, goodness, and usability in interactive products
authority: Hassenzahl originated the pragmatic/hedonic model of user experience.
caveats: Based on MP3 player skins; a 2008 web replication (Interacting with Computers) partly extended it.

title: Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression!
authority: Lindgaard is a leading HCI researcher; the paper launched the first-impression literature for websites.
caveats: Measures agreement of ratings across exposure times, not whether 50 ms impressions alter later behavior. The exact 50 ms vs 500 ms correlation coefficient was not confirmed; sources say only that it was high. Tuch et al. (2012) extended to 17 ms.

title: The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites: Working towards understanding aesthetic judgments
authority: Controlled experiments on complexity and prototypicality at 17 to 50 ms.
caveats: Screenshots of mostly Western sites; low complexity plus high prototypicality wins, which favors conventional design.

title: Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics with a quantification of perceived visual complexity and colorfulness
authority: CHI paper with 450 sites and 548 raters; computational models of perceived appeal.
caveats: Explains about half the variance at 500 ms; appeal varies with age, education and culture (Reinecke and Gajos 2014). DOI removed as not confirmed; pages 2049-2058 confirmed.

title: Prominence-interpretation theory: Explaining how people assess credibility online
container: CHI '03 Extended Abstracts on Human Factors in Computing Systems
authority: Fogg directed the Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab and the Stanford Web Credibility Project.
caveats: Two-page extended abstract; the large-sample data come from related Fogg et al. papers. Theory is descriptive and little tested on its interpretation component.

title: Trust and mistrust of online health sites
authority: Peer-reviewed CHI paper from Northumbria psychologists; origin of the staged trust model.
caveats: Small qualitative sample (15 women), health domain, UK.

title: Aesthetics and credibility in web site design
authority: Peer-reviewed experiment with same-content sites differing only in visual treatment.
caveats: Perceived credibility only, not accuracy. DOI removed as not confirmed; volume and pages confirmed via dblp.

title: Emotional design: Why we love (or hate) everyday things
authority: Norman is a founding figure of HCI and design; the book is the standard popular synthesis of affect and design.
caveats: Claims lean on Isen's positive affect studies, whose replicability has been questioned; the three-level model is a framework, not an empirically tested theory.

title: How do users evaluate the credibility of Web sites? A study with over 2,500 participants
container: Proceedings of the 2003 Conference on Designing for User Experiences (DUX '03)
authority: Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab web credibility study; the largest coded sample of why people trust or distrust sites.
caveats: Self-reported comments on two sites per person in a single category; shows what people say they notice, not what drives decisions. Pages not confirmed.
